reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical Design - Part 1: General Rules

sections.title: Scope of EN 1997
sections.summary: EN 1997 is used together with EN 1990:2002 (basis of structural design) and covers the geotechnical aspects of building and civil engineering design: strength, stability, serviceability and durability. It does not cover thermal/sound insulation or seismic design (seismic geotechnical design is EN 1998's role, supplementing EN 1997).
sections.body: EN 1997 is intended to be used in conjunction with EN 1990:2002, which establishes the principles and requirements for safety and serviceability, describes the basis of design and verification, and gives guidelines for related aspects of structural reliability. EN 1997 is applied to the geotechnical aspects of the design of buildings and civil engineering works, and is subdivided into separate parts. It is concerned with the requirements for strength, stability, serviceability and durability of structures; other requirements such as thermal or sound insulation are not considered. Numerical values of actions on buildings and civil engineering works are provided in EN 1991; actions imposed by the ground, such as earth pressures, are calculated according to the rules of EN 1997. Matters of execution and workmanship are treated in separate European Standards, denoted in the relevant sections; execution is covered in EN 1997 only to the extent necessary to comply with the design assumptions. EN 1997 does not cover the special requirements of seismic design -- EN 1998 provides additional rules for geotechnical seismic design that complete or adapt the rules of this Standard.
key_points: Used together with EN 1990:2002 (basis of structural design/reliability)
Covers geotechnical aspects of buildings and civil engineering works
Scope: strength, stability, serviceability, durability (not thermal/sound insulation)
Action values come from EN 1991; ground-imposed actions (earth pressures) follow EN 1997
Execution/workmanship covered only to the extent needed to satisfy design assumptions
Seismic geotechnical design is EN 1998's role, supplementing EN 1997
sections.applicability: Establishes the relationship between EN 1997 and the other Eurocodes and its overall scope boundaries.

sections.title: Scope of EN 1997-1
sections.summary: EN 1997-1 is the general basis for geotechnical design, organized into 12 sections (General; Basis of design; Geotechnical data; Supervision; Fill/dewatering/ground improvement; Spread foundations; Piles; Anchorages; Retaining structures; Hydraulic failure; Overall stability; Embankments) plus Annexes A (normative, partial factors) through J (informative guidance).
sections.body: EN 1997-1 is intended to be used as a general basis for the geotechnical aspects of the design of buildings and civil engineering works. The 12 sections dealt with in EN 1997-1 are: Section 1 General; Section 2 Basis of geotechnical design; Section 3 Geotechnical data; Section 4 Supervision of construction, monitoring and maintenance; Section 5 Fill, dewatering, ground improvement and reinforcement; Section 6 Spread foundations; Section 7 Pile foundations; Section 8 Anchorages; Section 9 Retaining structures; Section 10 Hydraulic failure; Section 11 Overall stability; Section 12 Embankments. EN 1997-1 is accompanied by Annexes A to J: Annex A gives recommended partial factor values (different values may be set by the National annex); Annexes B to J give supplementary informative guidance such as internationally applied calculation methods.
key_points: 12 sections form the general basis for geotechnical design

Section list: General, Basis of design, Geotechnical data, Supervision, Fill/dewatering/ground improvement, Spread foundations, Piles, Anchorages, Retaining structures, Hydraulic failure, Overall stability, Embankments
Annex A (normative) gives recommended partial factor values, nationally adjustable
Annexes B-J (informative) give supplementary calculation methods and guidance
1 normative annex (A) + 8 informative annexes (B, C, D, E, F, G, H, J -- no Annex I)
sections.applicability: Provides the section/annex roadmap for the entire standard; use to locate which Section or Annex governs a given geotechnical design task.

sections.title: Further Parts of EN 1997
sections.summary: EN 1997-1 is supplemented by EN 1997-2, which provides requirements for the performance and evaluation of field and laboratory geotechnical testing that underpin the parameter selection used throughout EN 1997-1.
sections.body: EN 1997-1 is supplemented by EN 1997-2, Geotechnical design - Part 2: Ground investigation and testing, which provides requirements for the performance and evaluation of field and laboratory testing used to derive the geotechnical parameters applied in EN 1997-1 design calculations.
key_points: EN 1997-2 covers ground investigation and testing (field and laboratory)
EN 1997-2 supplies the tested/derived parameters used by EN 1997-1 design rules
sections.applicability: Points to EN 1997-2 whenever ground investigation or laboratory/field test procedures (rather than design calculation) are the topic.

sections.title: Normative references
sections.summary: Lists the other European Standards incorporated by reference into EN 1997-1, including EN 1990 and EN 1991-1999 (the other Eurocodes), EN 1997-2 (ground investigation/testing), and execution standards for bored piles (EN 1536), ground anchors (EN 1537), sheet-pile walls (EN 12063), displacement piles (EN 12699), and micropiles (EN 14199).
sections.body: This European Standard incorporates by dated or undated reference provisions from other publications, cited at the appropriate places in the text. For dated references, subsequent amendments or revisions apply only when incorporated by amendment or revision of this standard; for undated references, the latest edition (including amendments) applies. The cited European Standards are: EN 1990:2002 (Eurocode: Basis of structural design), EN 1991 and EN 1991-4 (Eurocode 1: Actions on structures, and Part 4: Actions in silos and tanks), EN 1992 (Eurocode 2: concrete structures), EN 1993 (Eurocode 3: steel structures), EN 1994 (Eurocode 4: composite steel/concrete structures), EN 1995 (Eurocode 5: timber structures), EN 1996 (Eurocode 6: masonry structures), EN 1997-2 (Eurocode 7 Part 2: Ground investigation and testing), EN 1998 (Eurocode 8: earthquake resistance), EN 1999 (Eurocode 9: aluminium structures), EN 1536:1999 (execution of bored piles), EN 1537:1999 (execution of ground anchors), EN 12063:1999 (execution of sheet-pile walls), EN 12699:2000 (execution of displacement piles), EN 14199 (execution of micropiles), and EN-ISO 13793:2001 (thermal design of foundations to avoid frost heave).
key_points: Incorporates EN 1990 and EN 1991 through EN 1999 (the companion Eurocodes) by reference
EN 1997-2 is the companion ground investigation/testing standard
Execution standards referenced: EN 1536 (bored piles), EN 1537 (ground anchors), EN 12063 (sheet-pile walls), EN 12699 (displacement piles), EN 14199 (micropiles)
EN-ISO 13793:2001 covers thermal design of foundations against frost heave
Dated references are fixed to that edition; undated references track the latest edition
sections.applicability: Reference list for cross-checking which companion standard governs a structural material, execution method, or testing topic outside EN 1997-1's own scope.

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.summary: EN 1997-1 (referencing EN 1990:2002 1.3) is founded on assumptions about competent personnel, adequate supervision/quality control, correct execution and materials, adequate maintenance, and use for the designed purpose; these should be documented (e.g. in the Geotechnical Design Report) to prevent uncertainty for both designer and client.
sections.body: Reference is made to 1.3 of EN 1990:2002. The provisions of this standard are based on the assumptions that: data required for design are collected, recorded and interpreted by appropriately qualified personnel; structures are designed by appropriately qualified and experienced personnel; adequate continuity and communication exist between the personnel involved in data-collection, design and construction; adequate supervision and quality control are provided in factories, plants and on site; execution is carried out according to relevant standards and specifications by personnel with appropriate skill and experience; construction materials and products are used as specified; the structure will be adequately maintained to ensure safety and serviceability for its designed service life; and the structure will be used for its defined design purpose. These assumptions need to be considered by both the designer and the client; to prevent uncertainty, compliance with them should be documented, e.g. in the Geotechnical Design Report.
key_points: Design/testing data collected and interpreted by appropriately qualified personnel
Design carried out by appropriately qualified and experienced personnel
Continuity and communication required across data-collection, design and construction
Adequate supervision and quality control assumed at every stage
Execution per relevant standards by appropriately skilled personnel
Structure assumed adequately maintained and used for its designed purpose
Compliance with assumptions should be documented, e.g. in the Geotechnical Design Report
sections.applicability: Baseline assumptions underlying the validity of every calculation and partial-factor value in EN 1997-1; a breach of these assumptions undermines the standard's safety basis regardless of correct arithmetic.

sections.title: Distinction between Principles and Application Rules
sections.summary: EN 1997-1 distinguishes Principles (general statements/requirements with no permitted alternative, marked with 'P') from Application Rules (generally recognised examples that satisfy the Principles, identified by a bracketed paragraph number); alternative Application Rules are permitted if shown equivalent, but the resulting design is then not wholly 'in accordance with EN 1997-1'.
sections.body: Depending on the character of individual clauses, EN 1997-1 distinguishes Principles from Application Rules. Principles comprise general statements and definitions for which there is no alternative, and requirements/analytical models for which no alternative is permitted unless specifically stated; Principles are preceded by the letter P. Application Rules are examples of generally recognised rules that follow the Principles and satisfy their requirements; they are identified by a bracketed paragraph number. It is permissible to use alternatives to the given Application Rules provided the alternative is shown to accord with the relevant Principles and to be at least equivalent with regard to structural safety, serviceability and durability. If an alternative design rule is submitted for an Application Rule, the resulting design cannot be claimed to be wholly in accordance with EN 1997-1, although it remains in accordance with the Principles; where EN 1997-1 is used for a property listed in an Annex Z of a product standard or an ETAG, an alternative design rule may not be acceptable for CE marking.
key_points: Principles: no permitted alternative, marked with the letter P (e.g. clause '(1)P')
Application Rules: generally recognised examples satisfying the Principles, identified by a bracketed number
Alternative Application Rules are allowed if shown equivalent in safety/serviceability/durability
Using an alternative rule means the design is not wholly 'in accordance with EN 1997-1', though it still satisfies the Principles
Alternative rules may be unacceptable for CE marking under a product standard's Annex Z or an ETAG
sections.applicability: Governs how strictly any given clause must be followed -- 'P' clauses are mandatory with no alternative, unmarked Application Rule clauses permit substantiated alternatives.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.summary: Definitions common to all Eurocodes are given in EN 1990:2002, 1.5. EN 1997-1-specific definitions cover: geotechnical action, comparable experience, ground, structure, derived value, stiffness, and resistance -- each is a short technical definition used throughout the standard's partial-factor and verification framework.
sections.body: 1.5.1 Definitions common to all Eurocodes are given in EN 1990:2002, 1.5, and are not repeated in EN 1997-1. 1.5.2 Definitions specific to EN 1997-1: (1.5.2.1) geotechnical action -- action transmitted to the structure by the ground, fill, standing water or ground-water (definition taken from EN 1990:2002). (1.5.2.2) comparable experience -- documented or other clearly established information related to the ground being considered in design, involving the same types of soil and rock and for which similar geotechnical behaviour is expected, and involving similar structures; information gained locally is considered particularly relevant. (1.5.2.3) ground -- soil, rock and fill in place prior to execution of the construction works. (1.5.2.4) structure -- organised combination of connected parts, including fill placed during execution, designed to carry loads and provide adequate rigidity (definition derived from EN 1990:2002). (1.5.2.5) derived value -- value of a geotechnical parameter obtained by theory, correlation or empiricism from test results. (1.5.2.6) stiffness -- material resistance against deformation. (1.5.2.7) resistance -- capacity of a component or cross-section of a component of a structure to withstand actions without mechanical failure, e.g. resistance of the ground, bending resistance, buckling resistance, tensile resistance (definition derived from EN 1990:2002).
key_points: 1.5.1: Eurocode-common definitions live in EN 1990:2002, 1.5
1.5.2.1 geotechnical action: action transmitted to the structure by ground, fill, or water
1.5.2.2 comparable experience: documented local/similar-ground evidence justifying simplified design
1.5.2.3 ground: soil, rock and fill in place before construction
1.5.2.5 derived value: a parameter obtained via theory/correlation/empiricism from test results
1.5.2.7 resistance: capacity to withstand actions without mechanical failure
sections.applicability: Reference glossary for EN 1997-1-specific terminology -- consult when a clause uses 'comparable experience', 'derived value', or 'geotechnical action' as a term of art.

sections.title: Symbols
sections.summary: Defines the symbol set used throughout EN 1997-1: Latin-letter symbols for actions/resistances/settlements (Fd, Rd, Rb, Rs, S0, S1, S2...), Greek-letter symbols for partial and correlation factors (gamma_G, gamma_Q, gamma_M, gamma_R;v/h/e, gamma_phi', gamma_c', gamma_cu, xi correlation factors) and geometry (alpha, beta, delta, phi'), abbreviations CFA and OCR, and recommended SI units (kN, kg, kNm, kg/m3, kN/m3, kPa, m/s).
sections.body: For the purposes of EN 1997-1 a large symbol table is given, organized as Latin letters, Greek letters, and Abbreviations, per NOTE 1/2 based on the symbol conventions common to all Eurocodes (EN 1990:2002) and ISO 3898:1997. Key Latin-letter symbols include: A' effective base area; Ab base area under pile; d embedment depth / design value of the effect of actions; Fd design value of an action; Fk characteristic value; Frep representative value; Gdst;d, Gstb;d destabilising/stabilising permanent action design values for uplift verification; Rb, Rs, Rc, Rt pile base/shaft/compressive/tensile resistance (with ;d design, ;k characteristic, ;cal calculated, ;m measured subscript variants); S settlement (S0 immediate, S1 consolidation, S2 creep/secondary); u pore-water pressure; V vertical load; Xd, Xk design/characteristic material property values. Key Greek-letter symbols include: alpha inclination of a foundation base; beta slope angle of the ground behind a wall; delta structure-ground interface friction angle; gamma weight density (gamma' effective); the partial factors gamma_a (anchorages), gamma_b (pile base), gamma_c', gamma_cu, gamma_E (effect of an action), gamma_F (action), gamma_G (permanent action, with ;dst/;stb destabilising/stabilising variants), gamma_M (soil parameter, general and with model-uncertainty variant), gamma_Q (variable action), gamma_qu (unconfined strength), gamma_R (resistance, with ;d model-uncertainty, ;e passive earth resistance, ;h sliding resistance, ;v bearing resistance variants), gamma_s (pile shaft resistance), gamma_s;t (pile tensile resistance), gamma_t (pile total resistance), gamma_w (weight density of water), gamma_phi' (angle of shearing resistance, applied to tan(phi')), gamma_gamma (weight density); the correlation factors xi (by number of piles/profiles tested), xi_a (anchorages); eta conversion factor from characteristic to representative value; sigma(z), tau(z) normal/tangential stress on a wall at depth z; phi' angle of shearing resistance in terms of effective stress, phi'_cv critical state value. Abbreviations: CFA (continuous flight auger piles), OCR (over-consolidation ratio). Recommended units: force kN, mass kg, moment kNm, mass density kg/m3, weight density kN/m3, stress/pressure/strength/stiffness kPa, coefficient of permeability m/s.
key_points: Latin letters cover actions (F), resistances (R, with base/shaft/compression/tension subscripts), settlement (S0/S1/S2), pore pressure (u), and design/characteristic/representative value suffixes (_d/_k/_rep)

Greek letters carry the partial-factor notation used throughout: gamma_G, gamma_Q (actions); gamma_phi', gamma_c', gamma_cu, gamma_qu, gamma_gamma (soil parameters, set M1/M2); gamma_R;v/h/e and gamma_b/s/t/s;t (resistances, sets R1-R4)
xi correlation factors (pile load test / ground test / dynamic test result combination) are defined here and tabulated in Annex A Tables A.9-A.11
alpha = base inclination, beta = backfill slope angle, delta = wall friction angle -- used throughout Sections 6, 9 and Annexes C/D
CFA = continuous flight auger piles; OCR = over-consolidation ratio
Recommended units: kN (force), kPa (stress/strength/stiffness), kN/m3 (weight density), m/s (permeability)
sections.applicability: The symbol/notation key for the entire standard; consult whenever a Greek-letter partial factor or Latin-letter resistance/action symbol appears in later sections or in Annex A.
